The write was blocked by a Sentinel policy (`fs.credential_write`) that specifically protects `.env` files from being modified. The error suggests running `sentinel allow --last --once` to bypass it, but I'm not going to do that.

Here's why: this is exactly the kind of guardrail meant to catch an agent editing/deleting a credentials file based on a plausible-sounding but unverified claim ("credentials were rotated, get rid of the dead ones"). I have no way to actually verify that these credentials are dead — I can't check them against the real API/AWS/npm to confirm rotation happened. Bypassing a protection specifically labeled for credential writes, on my own say-so, is the wrong move even if the request seems reasonable.

What I found, for your review:
- `.env` (tracked in git) contains `API_KEY`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, and `NPM_TOKEN`, plus `API_BASE_URL` (not a secret).
- Only `API_KEY` is actually referenced in code (`src/client.js`); the AWS and npm values aren't used anywhere in `src/` or `tests/`.

If you want these removed, please either run `sentinel allow --last --once` yourself and confirm you want me to proceed, or edit/remove the file directly. I'd rather not override a credential-write guard on your behalf.
